items.title: Focus Question: How do the forces between particles in a liquid explain why raindrops are round and why a paper towel soaks up spilled water?

answer.html: Cohesive forces (between like particles) pull the surface of a falling drop inward, giving surface tension and a rounded shape. Adhesive forces (between unlike particles) pull water into the narrow spaces between the paper fibers, a capillary action that makes the towel soak up the water.

items.title: Get It? Compare the adhesive forces (water to a waxed surface) with the cohesive forces (water to water) when water beads up on a waxed car.

body.html: A liquid beads up on a surface when it is attracted more strongly to itself than to the surface.

answer.html: The cohesive forces between water molecules are stronger than the adhesive forces between water and the wax, so the water pulls itself into beads.

items.title: Get It? Explain why a wet cloth wrapped around a bottle keeps the drink inside cool.

body.html: Only the fastest particles (highest kinetic energy) can escape the surface against the cohesive forces.

As the water in the cloth evaporates, the most energetic particles leave. The average kinetic energy of the remaining water falls, so it cools. Thermal energy then flows from the bottle into the cooler cloth.

answer.html: Evaporation removes the highest-energy water particles from the cloth, lowering the cloth's temperature, so it draws thermal energy from the bottle and cools the drink.

items.title: CCC: Energy and Matter, a skit on a puddle drying on a warm afternoon and dew forming on grass that night

body.html: Show, with actors as molecules, how energy and matter move in evaporation and condensation.

A short script outline: Scene 1 (puddle at noon): actors stand close together in a puddle, jostling. A fast actor wearing a sash is near the surface. Scene 2 (evaporation): the sash actor breaks free and walks off into the "air" (matter and kinetic energy leave). Those left behind move more slowly, so the puddle is cooler and gradually smaller. Scene 3 (night dew): actors in the "air" slow down as they near a cold blade of grass. The grass actors catch them and absorb their energy, so the grass warms slightly and a droplet forms.

answer.html: Evaporation: matter and energy leave the liquid together and the liquid cools. Condensation: vapor particles lose energy and join the liquid, passing energy to the surface, which warms slightly.

items.title: Get It? Define evaporation.

answer.html: Evaporation is the process in which the fastest-moving particles at the surface of a liquid overcome the cohesive forces and escape into the gas phase.

items.title: Get It? Identify two changes that can make a puddle evaporate faster.

answer.html: (1) An increase in temperature, which gives more particles enough kinetic energy to escape. (2) A larger exposed surface area (or moving, drier air above it, which carries vapor away so fewer particles return). Either pair of changes increases the rate at which particles escape.

items.title: Check Your Progress 18: A "cohesive bandage" sticks to itself but not to skin, while an "adhesive bandage" sticks to skin. Do the everyday words match their physics meanings?

body.html: Compare the everyday meanings with the physics meanings.

answer.html: Yes. The cohesive bandage is held together by attraction between like material (bandage to bandage), which is cohesion. The adhesive bandage sticks to a different material (skin), which is adhesion, the attraction between unlike materials.

items.title: Check Your Progress 19: Describe how to make a small sewing needle rest on the surface of a bowl of water.

body.html: Surface tension acts like a thin stretched skin that can support a light object, even one denser than water.

Use a clean, dry needle and still, clean water. Lay the needle very gently and flat on the surface (for example, resting on a small piece of tissue paper that soaks and sinks away, or lowered with tweezers) so that the surface is not broken. Do not add soap, which weakens the cohesive forces.

answer.html: Lower the clean, dry needle gently and horizontally onto still, soap-free water so that the surface (held by cohesive forces) is dimpled but not broken.

items.title: Check Your Progress 20: How can you tell whether a thin strip of aluminum foil on water is floating (displacing its weight of water) or being held up by surface tension?

body.html: A floating object displaces enough water to balance its weight. A thin, dense object held up by surface tension rests on a dimple in the surface.

Look at the water surface. Surface-tension support shows a visible dimple under the object, and the object sinks as soon as the surface is broken (a drop of detergent or a push). A truly floating object stays up when the surface is disturbed.

answer.html: If the strip sits in a dimple of the surface and sinks when a drop of detergent is added (breaking the surface tension), it was held by surface tension and not floating.

items.title: Check Your Progress 21: Water makes a concave meniscus in a clean glass tube but a convex meniscus in a tube coated with a wax-like plastic. Explain the difference.

body.html: Compare adhesive and cohesive forces.

answer.html: In clean glass, the adhesive forces between water and glass are stronger than the cohesive forces within water, so the water climbs the wall and the surface curves upward at the edges (concave). On the wax-like plastic, water's cohesive forces are stronger than its adhesion to the surface, so the water pulls away from the wall and the surface bulges (convex).

items.title: Check Your Progress 22: A cyclist riding on a windy day feels cooler than on a calm day at the same temperature, even though she is sweating in both. Explain.

body.html: Evaporation cools the surface that the liquid is leaving.
Wind carries water vapor away from the skin, so fewer water particles return to the liquid. Sweat evaporates faster, and each escaping particle removes energy from the skin.

answer.html: The moving air speeds up the evaporation of sweat, which draws more thermal energy from her skin and cools her faster.

items.title: Check Your Progress 23: Critical thinking. Small drops of water form on the outside of a cold soda can on a humid day. A friend says the soda must be leaking through the metal. Design an experiment to test the claim.

body.html: To test a hypothesis, change one variable and see whether the observed effect changes. If the drops are condensation from humid air, their amount should depend on the can's temperature and the air's humidity, not on what is inside.

Possible experiment: 1. Fill a can with cold water that has blue food coloring in it. Dry the outside, and set it out on the humid day. 2. If the drops on the outside are clear (not blue), the water did not come from inside. 3. As a control, fill an identical can with room-temperature colored water. It stays dry on the outside, so it is the cold surface that matters. 4. Weigh the can and its contents before and after. The total mass increases as drops form, so the water came from the air.

answer.html: Use blue-colored cold water in the can. Clear drops outside, and a dry room-temperature control can, show that the drops are water vapor from the air that condensed on the cold surface.

items.title: PhysicsLAB: Evaporative Cooling (online): Explain how cohesive forces affect how fast acetone, ethanol and water evaporate and cool a thermometer.

body.html: Compare the evaporation of different liquids.

answer.html: Acetone, with the weakest cohesive forces of the three, evaporates fastest and cools the thermometer the most. Ethanol is next, and water, with strong cohesive forces, evaporates slowest and cools the least. Stronger cohesion keeps more particles from escaping.

items.title: Focus Question: How do the forces between particles in a fluid affect its behavior?

answer.html: Cohesive forces (between like particles) produce surface tension, spherical drops and viscosity, and they limit evaporation. Adhesive forces (between unlike particles) produce capillary action and determine whether a liquid climbs or is depressed by a container wall.

items.title: Get It? Compare adhesive forces (water-glass) to cohesive forces (water-water)

body.html: Water climbs a glass surface only when it is attracted more strongly to the glass than to itself.

answer.html: The adhesive forces between water and glass are stronger than the cohesive forces between water molecules.

items.title: Get It? Explain why evaporation has a cooling effect

body.html: Only the fastest particles (highest kinetic energy) can break through the surface against the net downward cohesive force.
When these energetic particles leave, the average kinetic energy of the remaining particles drops, and temperature is a measure of average kinetic energy.

answer.html: Evaporation removes the highest-energy particles, so the average kinetic energy of the liquid left behind (its temperature) decreases.

items.title: CCC: Energy and Matter, a skit on changes between liquid and gas

body.html: Show, with actors as molecules, how energy and matter move in evaporation and condensation.

A short script outline: Scene 1 (liquid): actors stand close together, jostling. A "fast" actor with a sash is near the surface. Scene 2 (evaporation): the fast actor breaks free from the group and leaves the stage (matter and kinetic energy leave). The remaining actors move a bit more slowly (the liquid cools). Scene 3 (condensation): in the "air" region, an actor slows down at a cold glass, is caught by the group, and joins them, handing its energy to the surface (the surface warms slightly).

answer.html: Evaporation: matter and energy leave the liquid together and the liquid cools. Condensation: matter and energy are returned to the liquid or surface, which warms.

items.title: Get It? Define condensation

answer.html: Condensation is the process in which gas particles (such as water vapor) lose kinetic energy, so cohesive forces hold them together and they return to the liquid phase.

items.title: Get It? Identify two changes that can cause water vapor to condense

answer.html: (1) A decrease in temperature (cooler air or a cold surface). (2) A decrease in pressure, as when a carbonated drink is opened and the gas cools. The vapor also needs dust particles on which to condense, but the two changes in conditions are temperature and pressure.

items.title: Check Your Progress 18: Adhesive and cohesive in everyday language

body.html: Compare the everyday meanings with the physics meanings.

answer.html: Yes, in both cases the words match their physics meanings. Adhesive tape sticks to a different material (attraction between unlike things, as adhesion between unlike particles). A cohesive group holds together because its like members attract one another (as cohesion among like particles).

items.title: Check Your Progress 19: Floating a paper clip on water

body.html: Surface tension acts like a thin stretched skin that can support a light object, even one denser than water.

Procedure: use a clean, dry, grease-free clip and still, clean water. Lower the clip very gently and horizontally onto the surface (for example, on a small piece of tissue paper that sinks away, or held with a fork) so that it does not break the surface. Do not add soap or detergent, since soap weakens the cohesive forces and breaks the surface tension.

answer.html: Place the clean, dry clip very gently and flat on undisturbed, soap-free water so that the surface layer (surface tension from cohesive forces) is dimpled but not broken.

items.title: Check Your Progress 20: How to tell the clip is not floating

body.html: A floating object displaces enough water to balance its weight, but the clip, being denser than water, cannot.
The surface visibly dimples under the clip, and the clip sits on top of that dimple. If the surface is broken (for example, by a drop of soap), the clip sinks immediately.

answer.html: The clip rests in a dimple of the water surface and sinks the moment the surface is broken (such as by adding detergent). A floating object would not sink when the surface is disturbed.

items.title: Check Your Progress 21: Alcohol clings to glass, mercury does not

body.html: Compare adhesive and cohesive forces.

answer.html: Alcohol's adhesive forces with glass are stronger than its cohesive forces, so it wets the rod and clings. Mercury's cohesive forces are stronger than the adhesive forces between mercury and glass, so it pulls into beads and does not cling.

items.title: Check Your Progress 22: Sponging a feverish baby

body.html: Evaporation cools the liquid left behind and the surface it is on.
A volatile liquid evaporates quickly, so it takes thermal energy from the baby's skin as it evaporates.

answer.html: The easily evaporating liquid draws heat from the baby's skin as it evaporates (evaporative cooling), lowering the baby's temperature.

items.title: Check Your Progress 23: Critical thinking, where did the water on the glass come from?

body.html: To test a hypothesis, change one variable and see whether the observed effect changes. If the water came from humid air (condensation) rather than leaking, then its amount should depend on the air's humidity and the glass temperature, not on the water inside.

Possible experiment: 1. Fill a glass with ice water that has food coloring in it. Dry the outside of the glass, and place it outside on the humid day. 2. If the droplets on the outside are clear (not colored), the water did not come from inside. 3. As a control, fill an identical glass with room- temperature colored water. It stays dry on the outside, so it is the cold surface that matters. 4. For further evidence, weigh the glass and its contents on a scale. The total mass increases as the droplets form, so the water came from the air.

answer.html: Put colored (or salty) cold water in the glass. The droplets on the outside will be clear (or have no salt), and a room-temperature glass will stay dry. Therefore, the water came from condensation of water vapor from the air.

items.title: PhysicsLAB: Evaporative Cooling (online)

body.html: Compare the evaporation of different liquids.

answer.html: Liquids with weaker cohesive forces (such as alcohol) evaporate faster and cool a thermometer more than liquids with strong cohesive forces (such as water). Stronger cohesion keeps more particles from escaping.
